title: Architecture Patterns
tagline: From monolith to microservices — the structural patterns that shape how systems are built, deployed, and scaled.

sections.content:
Architecture is the set of decisions that are hardest to change later. Should the application be one deployable unit or dozens? Should services call each other directly or through an intermediary? Should work happen synchronously or via a queue? Getting these decisions wrong at scale means rewrites measured in engineer-years.

The good news: a small set of **patterns** covers 90% of real systems. Client-server, monolith vs microservices, load balancing, API gateway, and message queues are the vocabulary every senior engineer reasons in. Master the trade-offs and you can evaluate any architecture diagram in minutes.

sections.caption: A microservices system: the API gateway is the single entry point, the load balancer distributes traffic, and the message queue decouples async work.

sections.title: Restaurant Kitchen Models
sections.content: A **monolith** is a single open kitchen where every chef shares the same tools, stove, and pantry. Coordination is easy but one broken stove shuts everyone down. **Microservices** are separate food stations — sushi, grill, pastry — each with dedicated tools. The head waiter (API gateway) routes orders to the right station, and a ticket rail (message queue) lets the grill station fire dessert orders to pastry without waiting. More moving parts, but one broken fryer only kills the fries.

**Client-server** is the foundational pattern: clients request resources, servers fulfill them. The HTTP protocol formalized this split. Every web application, mobile app, and API is a client-server system. The variant matters: thin client (all logic server-side) vs thick client (SPA with API) changes where you deploy, cache, and scale.

**Monolith vs microservices** is the most consequential architectural choice. A monolith deploys as one unit: simple to develop, test, and debug; one process, one database. Microservices split by business domain: each service owns its data, deploys independently, and scales independently. The cost is distributed systems complexity — network latency, partial failures, distributed tracing, and eventual consistency. The rule of thumb: **start monolith, extract services when pain is real**. Netflix, Amazon, and Uber all started monolithic.

An **API gateway** is the single entry point for all client requests. It handles cross-cutting concerns — authentication, rate limiting, SSL termination, request routing, response transformation — so individual services don't each implement them. A **message queue** (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) decouples producers from consumers: the order service publishes an event and continues; the notification service, fulfillment service, and analytics service each consume it independently and at their own pace. This enables **async work**, prevents cascading failures, and naturally buffers traffic spikes.

sections.caption: Request flow: the gateway validates auth before forwarding. The order service responds to the client immediately, then publishes an async event — the notification service processes it independently.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The gateway handles auth and rate limiting once, then proxies the request to the correct microservice. Downstream services trust the `x-user-id` header injected by the gateway rather than validating tokens themselves — a clean separation of concerns.

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
# Docker Compose snippet — monolith vs microservices structure

# MONOLITH: one service, one database
services:
  app:
    image: my-monolith:latest
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
  db:
    image: postgres:16

# MICROSERVICES: each service is independent
services:
  api-gateway:
    image: gateway:latest
    ports: ["80:80"]
  auth-service:
    image: auth:latest       # deploys independently
  order-service:
    image: orders:latest     # scales independently
  orders-db:
    image: postgres:16       # own database per service
  queue:
    image: rabbitmq:3-management  # async decoupling

sections.content: The biggest microservices mistake is extracting services too early. Two-pizza teams at Amazon run dozens of services because they have the tooling, on-call rotations, and deployment automation to support them. A 3-person startup that splits into 10 microservices on day one ships 10x slower. Let the monolith show you where the seams are, then cut.

items: **Client-server** is the fundamental pattern: clients request, servers respond — every HTTP app is a client-server system.
**Monolith** is simpler to build and debug; microservices give independent deployability and scaling at the cost of distributed systems complexity.
**API gateway** centralizes cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, routing) so individual services stay focused on business logic.
**Message queues** decouple producers from consumers, enabling async processing, traffic buffering, and resilience to downstream failures.
**Load balancers** distribute traffic across multiple instances of the same service, enabling horizontal scaling and automatic failover.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of an API gateway over having clients call microservices directly?
options: It makes requests faster by caching every response
It centralizes cross-cutting concerns like auth and rate limiting in one place
It eliminates the need for a load balancer
It automatically converts REST to GraphQL
quiz.explanation: Without a gateway, every service must implement auth, rate limiting, and SSL termination independently. The gateway handles these once, keeping services focused on domain logic.

quiz.question: A message queue decouples services primarily by:
options: Sharing a single database between producer and consumer
Allowing the producer to call the consumer synchronously
Letting the producer publish an event and continue without waiting for the consumer
Replacing HTTP with a binary protocol for faster communication
quiz.explanation: The core value of a message queue is temporal decoupling: the producer publishes and moves on. The consumer processes the event when it is ready, at its own pace, and can even be offline when the event is published.

quiz.question: Which architecture pattern is generally recommended for a new startup's first product?
options: Microservices — for future scalability
Serverless — cheapest operational cost
Monolith — simplest to build, test, and iterate on
Event-driven — avoids synchronous coupling from day one
quiz.explanation: Monoliths are faster to build and easier to debug early on. The advice 'start monolith, extract services when the pain is real' is endorsed by practitioners at Amazon, Netflix, and Shopify — all of whom started monolithic.

quiz.question: In the request-flow diagram, why does the Order Service respond 201 to the client BEFORE the Notification Service processes the event?
options: The notification service is broken
HTTP responses must arrive before any async work can start
Async via message queue decouples the response from downstream processing
The gateway buffers the response until all services finish
quiz.explanation: The order service publishes to the queue and immediately returns 201. The client gets a fast response; the notification service processes the event asynchronously afterward. This pattern improves latency and resilience.

quiz.question: A load balancer sitting in front of three identical API servers primarily provides:
options: Database connection pooling
SSL certificate generation
Traffic distribution and automatic failover if one server goes down
API request validation and schema enforcement
quiz.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across healthy backend instances (horizontal scaling) and stops routing to an instance that fails health checks (automatic failover).

quiz.question: What does it mean for microservices to own their own data?
options: Each service runs its own authentication database
Each service has its own dedicated database; other services access its data via the service's API
Services share one database but use separate schemas
Data is replicated to every service for low latency
quiz.explanation: The 'database per service' pattern means no direct cross-service DB queries. Service B must call Service A's API to read A's data. This enforces loose coupling and lets each service evolve its schema independently.

quiz.question: SSL termination at the API gateway means:
options: All internal microservice communication is also HTTPS
The gateway decrypts HTTPS and forwards plain HTTP to internal services
The gateway rejects requests without client certificates
SSL is only applied to authentication endpoints
quiz.explanation: SSL termination at the gateway means the gateway handles the HTTPS handshake and decryption. Traffic between gateway and internal services can be plain HTTP on a private network, reducing TLS overhead on each service.

quiz.question: The 'two-pizza team' rule at Amazon means each microservice team should:
options: Be small enough to be fed by two pizzas — roughly 5-8 people
Ship two features per sprint to justify service overhead
Maintain two replicas of their service at all times
Deploy twice a day using CI/CD
quiz.explanation: Jeff Bezos's two-pizza rule means a team small enough that two pizzas could feed them — roughly 5-8 people. Small teams own and operate a small number of services, maximizing autonomy and minimizing coordination overhead.

quiz.question: In a monolith, what is the main reason one bug can cause a full system outage?
options: Monoliths always share a single database table
All modules run in the same process; a crash or OOM takes down the entire application
Monoliths cannot be load balanced
Deployments require shutting down all users simultaneously
quiz.explanation: A monolith is a single deployable process. An unhandled exception, memory leak, or crash in any one module terminates the whole process, bringing down all functionality at once.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical responsibility of an API gateway?
options: Rate limiting requests per client
Routing requests to the correct backend service
Storing and querying business data
Verifying authentication tokens
quiz.explanation: An API gateway handles cross-cutting infrastructure concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting, SSL. It does not store or query business data — that is the responsibility of the individual services and their databases.
